Article Title: Tough road for Trump: Why sanctions Bill for tariffs on Russian oil buyers may fail House test
Article Text:
Sanctions and trade experts say it would establish a new precedent by allowing future presidents to use secondary tariffs to target entire countries. (AP photo)

More power for Trump: Why are lawmakers concerned?

What is the US Senate Bill on Russia Sanctions?

Bill to face hurdles?

New precedents on sanctions

US President Donald Trump may not find it easy to get the new bill championing fresh sanctions on Russia and countries that trade with it passed. The proposed legislation would sanction Russian officials and authorise up to 100% tariffs on the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or natural gas, as well as the five countries considered to be the biggest enablers of Moscow's efforts to bypass US sanctions and continue financing its war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year.The Russia sanctions bill pushed for more than a year by the late Senator Lindsey Graham is facing growing resistance in Congress, with Democrats and some Republicans objecting to provisions that would give President Donald Trump sweeping new tariff powers, according to a Reuters report.Lawmakers from both parties, along with industry trade groups, have raised concerns over a section of the legislation that would allow Trump to impose hefty tariffs on countries that buy significant volumes of Russian oil and gas or on nations that his administration determines are helping Russia evade sanctions.While the bill does not identify those countries by name, they would likely include China, India and possibly certain European nations and Japan.Before his sudden death earlier this month, Graham had spent more than a year pushing for the measure. He secured Trump's backing only in recent weeks, as the Republican president became increasingly supportive of Ukraine while growing more frustrated with Moscow, the Reuters report said.The tariff provisions gained added significance for the White House after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's 10% to 50% "reciprocal" tariffs in February, prompting the administration to look for alternative legal authority to impose such trade measures.Also Read | India faces 100% Trump tariff threat as US Senate advances Russia Sanctions Bill - what it means The legislation also gives the president the authority to waive Russia-related sanctions for unspecified national security reasons. That provision has drawn opposition from pro-Ukraine Democrats, who cite Trump's changing positions on Russia and Ukraine.In addition, the bill would renew for another five years the Iran energy and weapons sanctions first enacted in 1996, which are due to expire this year. That extension was included as a condition for securing Trump's support. Earlier this week, Trump also insisted that tariffs on Iran be added to the legislation, despite the fact that trade between the US and Iran is virtually non-existent.With opinion polls indicating that Democrats could regain control of the House of Representatives and potentially the Senate in the November congressional elections, some lawmakers believe it would be better to delay passage of the Russia sanctions bill until Democrats have greater influence over legislation that many consider unprecedented, the report said.The legislation received overwhelming bipartisan backing in procedural votes in the US Senate on Tuesday and Wednesday, with lawmakers describing it as a tribute to the late Senator Lindsey Graham.Congressional aides said the bill could be approved by the full Senate before lawmakers leave Washington for their home states next week.However, the measure, which has been renamed in Graham's honour, is expected to face a tougher path in the House of Representatives, which is in recess until August 31.Opposition has already emerged from some senior Democrats.Senator Ron Wyden and Representative Richard Neal, the ranking Democrats on the Senate and House trade committees, criticised the legislation, arguing that it would hand Trump broad new tariff powers that could push up inflation in the United States."There is no question that the US ‌government must take ⁠stronger action against purchasers of Russian energy who are fueling the unjustifiable war against Ukraine. But the latest draft of the Sanctioning Russia Act is a prescription for bedlam and higher tariffs," they said in a joint statement.The bill has also sparked concerns among some Republicans.Mahur Patel, a former Republican congressional aide who is now with the Hogan Lovells Cadwalader law firm, said he was sceptical that the legislation would pass the House this year, citing the approaching election season and continued unease among Republicans over the scope of Trump's tariff policies.According to Patel, many Republican lawmakers remain uncomfortable with Trump's earlier sweeping tariffs, with some continuing to press for product-specific exemptions, such as the temporary relief granted this week for phosphate fertiliser imports from Morocco to prevent shortages linked to the Iran war.Apart from concerns that the legislation could add to inflationary pressures in the United States, sanctions and trade experts say it would establish a new precedent by allowing future presidents to use secondary tariffs to target entire countries, rather than limiting action to individuals or entities accused of helping evade sanctions.Although the bill specifies that these powers would expire after five years, experts note that governments rarely relinquish authorities once they have been granted.Supporters of the legislation maintain that the five-year sunset provision sufficiently limits the tariff authority, allowing it to curb Russia's energy revenues without creating broader unintended consequences.Jess Hoversen, a former senior US government official who is now chief economist at developer platform bank Column, said the legislation would, if enacted, hand the government an extremely broad tool capable of affecting entire bilateral trade relationships."Secondary tariffs, as designed in this bill, would function as a much blunter instrument that could apply across-the-board duties to all goods from a country based on its energy trade with Russia or its role in sanctions evasion," Hoversen said.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump may not find it easy to get the new bill championing fresh sanctions on Russia and countries that trade with it passed. The proposed legislation would sanction Russian officials and authorise up to 100% tariffs on the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or natural gas. Lawmakers from both parties, along with industry trade groups, have raised concerns over a section of the legislation.

Article Title: US stock market today: Nasdaq rises as Amazon rallies strongly
Article Text:
Market participants had viewed this week as a crucial test for the technology sector.

US stock market today: Nasdaq outperformed the other major Wall Street indexes on Friday as a 13.7% rally in Amazon shares lifted technology stocks. Amazon joined other Big Tech firms in reporting robust cloud business growth, easing investor concerns over returns from heavy artificial intelligence spending.At 9:47 a.m. ET, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 82.26 points, or 0.16%, at 52,290.32. The S&P 500 gained 10.05 points, or 0.12%, to 7,446.54, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced 86.20 points, or 0.34%, to 25,208.37.The S&P 500 consumer discretionary sector led the market, rising 5.2%, driven largely by Amazon's sharp gains, according to a Reuters report.Tech stocks in focusMarket participants had viewed this week as a crucial test for the technology sector. After a strong finish to the second quarter, AI-linked stocks came under pressure in July as investors locked in profits and waited for evidence that substantial AI investments were beginning to translate into meaningful returns despite weaker free cash flow.Amazon on Thursday reported its strongest quarterly revenue growth in more than four years, following similar results from Microsoft and Alphabet earlier this month.The performance encouraged investors to focus on the companies' accelerating growth rather than the sharp decline in free cash flow reported alongside the earnings."Amazon showed us, without a shadow of a doubt, that the web-services or AI side of the business is driving growth for the company," said Adam Sarhan, chief executive of 50 Park Investments in New York according to Reuters."Investors are able to look past the free-cash-flow decline because it is one component. If growth continues, it will make up for that shortfall."However, gains were tempered by Apple, whose shares fell 9.8% in early trade after the company cautioned that supply constraints would weigh on growth. Investors looked beyond the near-term shortages to assess the impact of an anticipated increase in iPhone prices.Microsoft shares rose 1.8% after recording their biggest single-day gain on record in the previous session. Alphabet and Meta each advanced more than 2%, while among semiconductor stocks, Nvidia climbed 1.3% and Micron added 1.6%.Despite the late-week rebound putting all three major Wall Street indexes on course for weekly gains, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq remained on track to end July in negative territory after AI-related stocks experienced a steep selloff during the month.The week also introduced fresh uncertainty over the interest-rate outlook after the Federal Reserve kept its benchmark rate unchanged. Comments from Chair Kevin Warsh, along with a broadly benign inflation report released on Thursday, prompted traders to raise the probability of rates remaining unchanged in September to 35%, compared with about 18% a week earlier, according to CME's FedWatch tool.
Article Summary: Nasdaq outperformed the other major Wall Street indexes on Friday as a 13.7% rally in Amazon shares lifted technology stocks. Amazon joined other Big Tech firms in reporting robust cloud business growth, easing investor concerns over returns from heavy artificial intelligence spending.

Article Title: US economy slows as GDP growth slips to 1.5%, consumers keep momentum alive
Article Text:
Imports emerge as the biggest drag

Inflation eases but stays above target

Resilience amid economic and political pressures

Strong consumer spending and steady business investment helped cushion the US economy in the second quarter, but a surge in imports dragged overall growth to its slowest pace this year, even as inflation showed further signs of easing.Data released by the commerce department on Thursday showed that the world's largest economy grew at an annual rate of 1.5% between April and June, slowing from 2.1% in the first quarter and coming in below economists' expectations.Household spending remained the biggest support for the economy during the quarter. Consumer spending, which accounts for about 70% of US economic activity, accelerated sharply to a 3.2% annual pace from just 0.5% in the January-March period.A broader measure of the economy's underlying strength also pointed to resilience. Excluding the volatile effects of government spending and trade, the economy expanded at a 3.9% annual rate, improving from 1.7% in the previous quarter.Businesses also continued to invest despite slower headline growth. Investment outside the housing sector increased at an annual pace of 8.4%, down from 10.6% in the first quarter but remaining strong, reflecting a surge in artificial intelligence-related investment.The biggest drag on growth came from imports, which climbed at an annual rate of 11.5%. Increased shipments of computer chips and other products supporting AI investment contributed to the rise. Because GDP measures only what is produced within the United States, imports are deducted from the calculation, reducing second-quarter growth by 1.5 percentage points."The consumer rescued the quarter,'' said Olu Sonola, head of US economics at Fitch Ratings. “AI investment remains a powerful growth story, but the import surge underpinning the buildout is a reminder that an AI boom does not automatically translate into an equally large boost to US GDP.”Alongside the GDP figures, the commerce department reported that inflation continued to cool in June, although it remained above the Federal Reserve's target.The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed's preferred measure of inflation, rose 3.7% from June 2025, easing from a 4.1% year-on-year increase in May. Core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, stood at 3.3%, compared with 3.4% in May.On a monthly basis, prices fell 0.1% between May and June, helped by a 9.2% decline in gasoline and other energy prices.Even so, inflation has remained above the central bank's 2% target for more than five years, frustrating policymakers as well as consumers facing a high cost of living ahead of the November midterm elections, now less than 100 days away.The Federal Reserve on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate unchanged for the fifth consecutive meeting. However, three regional Fed presidents dissented, saying they wanted to raise rates to tackle elevated inflation.The latest figures also highlighted the resilience of the US economy despite the Iran war and the spike in energy prices it triggered. The labour market has strengthened this year after a weak 2025, giving consumers the confidence and income to keep spending.Employers have added an average of 92,000 jobs a month this year, compared with fewer than 10,000 jobs a month in 2025, when high interest rates and President Donald Trump's erratic use of tariffs discouraged businesses from hiring.Political attention remains firmly on the economy ahead of November's midterm elections, which will determine whether President Donald Trump's Republicans retain full control of Congress.A new AP-NORC poll found public opinion has become less favourable towards the Iran war. It also showed that 72% of US adults consider it "extremely" or "very" important to prevent domestic oil and gas prices from rising, up from 67% in March.
Article Summary: US economy grew at an annual rate of 1.5% between April and June, slowing from 2.1% in the first quarter. Consumer spending, which accounts for about 70% of US economic activity, accelerated sharply to a 3.2% annual pace.

Article Title: US stock market today: Wall Street flat; Nasdaq climbs over 1.5% as tech stocks rally
Article Text:
In commodity markets, oil prices eased after recent sharp swings driven by escalating tensions in the Middle East.

US stock market today: Wall Street rebounded on Thursday, led by a sharp rally in Microsoft after the technology giant posted stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings. The S&P 500 rose 0.9%, recovering more than half of Wednesday's decline, its steepest fall in seven weeks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 250 points, or 0.5%, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.8%, a day after slipping 9.8% below the record high it reached last month.Microsoft surged 15.2% after reporting quarterly profit that exceeded analysts' expectations, supported by robust growth in its Azure cloud business. Chief Executive Satya Nadella said the performance reflected customers' increasing adoption of Microsoft's AI offerings. Investors also welcomed the company's decision not to significantly raise its AI spending plans, easing concerns that heavy investments in artificial intelligence could strain cash flows without delivering the expected gains in productivity and profitability.In contrast, Meta Platforms dropped 8.9% after reporting quarterly earnings that fell short of forecasts, despite revenue slightly exceeding expectations.Some analysts pointed to the company's decision to raise the lower end of its projected capital spending range for the year as a factor behind the decline.Chipmakers and memory manufacturers recovered some of their recent losses, as investors returned to stocks that had been hit by concerns over stretched valuations following the AI-driven rally. Micron Technology rose 8.4%, reducing its weekly decline to 13%, while Lam Research jumped 18.3% and Advanced Micro Devices advanced 7.3%.Broader markets also drew support from easing Treasury yields after Wednesday's sharp rise. The yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury slipped to 4.65% from 4.67%, while the 30-year Treasury yield remained at 5.20% after climbing from 5.09% the previous day.Treasury yields had surged after Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh offered few indications about the central bank's next steps to tackle persistently high inflation. While elevated interest rates help curb inflation, they also weigh on economic growth and reduce the appeal of equities and other risk assets.Economic data released on Thursday showed the US economy expanded more slowly than economists had expected during the spring. Inflation remained above the Federal Reserve's target in the latest month, although it came in slightly below market expectations.In commodity markets, oil prices eased after recent sharp swings driven by escalating tensions in the Middle East. Brent crude, the global benchmark, fell 1.5% to $86.79 a barrel. Prices have fluctuated dramatically this month, falling to as low as $72 before rising to $102 last week amid uncertainty over whether the United States and Iran could reach an agreement allowing oil tankers to move freely from the Middle East to global markets.
Article Summary: The S&P 500 rose 0.9%, recovering more than half of Wednesday's decline. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 250 points, or 0.5%, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.8%. Microsoft surged 15.2% after reporting quarterly profit that exceeded analysts' expectations.

Article Title: Asian stocks trade mixed after Fed holds rates; Kospi rallies 4%, Shenzhen slips 300 points
Article Text: Asian equities showed signs of stabilising on Thursday, but investors remained cautious after a turbulent week marked by a sharp AI-driven market sell-off, uncertainty over the US interest rate outlook and renewed geopolitical tensions that briefly sent oil prices soaring.Taiwan's benchmark climbed 666.47 points to 40,705.65, up 1.66%, while South Korea's Kospi gained 201.22 points to 5,864.46, rising 3.55%. Japan's Nikkei rose 881.37 points to 62,315.56, up 1.43%. Even so, the Nikkei was still headed for a weekly decline of 3%, while the Kospi remained on track for a 12% fall.In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng slipped 34.84 points to 25,773.08, down 0.13% around 8 am IST. In China, Shanghai lost 12.14 points to 3,816.329, down 0.32%, while Shenzhen declined 299.165 points to 13,359.279, falling 2.19%.Elsewhere, Australia's ASX 200 fell 0.48%, Singapore's STI eased 0.64% and Malaysia's benchmark was down 0.15%. New Zealand's NZX 50 dropped 1.43%.The sharp correction in South Korean equities has been at the centre of investor concerns this week after more than $2 trillion was wiped off the country's stock market.The sell-off, concentrated in chipmakers, has fuelled worries over whether the massive investments being made in artificial intelligence will generate adequate returns.The decline was severe enough for Finance Minister Koo Yun-cheol to apologise for the introduction of single-stock leveraged ETFs."Given that the fundamental thesis remains intact, there does appear to be an irrational, panic-like element to the current selling," Gina Kim, portfolio manager for emerging market equities at Nordea Asset Management in Singapore told Reuters."I cannot comment on when the panic will stop as such but some indicators to look out for would be margin balances in both Taiwan and Korea for retail investors. Both are declining but we would ideally need to see some levelling off," said Kim.Samsung Electronics offered some support to market sentiment after reporting a record second-quarter operating profit, up 19-fold from a year earlier.In commodities, Brent crude slipped back below $90 a barrel after jumping more than 7% in the previous session as fighting in the Middle East intensified. Despite continued missile and drone attacks, tanker traffic out of the region has continued, according to available data, easing some immediate supply concerns.The Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged, but its policy decision did little to settle markets. Instead, the split within the central bank left investors debating whether further rate hikes remain on the table.The uncertainty was reflected in the bond market, where longer-dated treasury yields climbed to their highest levels in 19 years. The 30-year treasury yield stood at 5.2039% after touching 5.2273%, its highest level since June 2007. The dollar also weakened following the policy announcement.At his post-meeting press conference, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh reiterated the central bank's commitment to tackling inflation but refrained from signalling its next move. He pointed to the rise in bond yields since the previous policy meeting, saying markets had already priced in tighter financial conditions, while noting that did not necessarily require the Fed to act.

Japan's Nikkei rose 881.37 points to 62,315.56, up1.43%. Even so, theNikkei was still headed for a weekly decline of 3%. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng slipped 34.84 points to 25,773.08.

Article Title: Crude prices retreat as oil continues flowing through Hormuz alternatives
Article Text: After a dramatic rally in the previous session, oil prices retreated on Thursday as crude continued to move out of the Middle East even as the US-Iran war widened beyond its primary battlefronts.WTI crude slipped 0.54% to $84.00 a barrel, while Brent crude fell 0.85% to $89.97 a barrel.The decline followed a sharp rebound on Wednesday, when Brent jumped 7.91% and WTI gained 6.56%. The gains had erased the losses from Tuesday, when both benchmarks had dropped about 5% after hostilities briefly paused in the five-month conflict.Even as tensions intensified, shipping activity suggested that oil supplies were still finding routes out of the region. Preliminary data showed 39 commodity vessels entered the Red Sea through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Tuesday, the highest number recorded since July 19. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, however, remained limited."While overall volumes are reduced, oil continues to leak out of the region through multiple channels, and additional workarounds are being explored. The longer this situation persists, the more these alternative routes and methods will erode Iran's leverage over the Strait of Hormuz," IG market analyst Tony Sycamore said in a note cited by Reuters.The Strait of Hormuz, which previously handled around one-fifth of global oil and gas flows, has remained largely blocked since the US-Iran war began in February, despite diplomatic efforts aimed at reopening the waterway.A senior Iranian official said Tehran had rejected an Omani proposal for regional joint management of the strategic passage.Military action in the region also intensified. US-Saudi strikes targeted Iran-backed paramilitary forces in Iraq on Wednesday, marking the first publicly acknowledged participation by Saudi Arabia in US air strikes. The operation was carried out in response to drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities launched from Iraq.The strikes marked the return of US military action in the Middle East after President Donald Trump halted a bombing campaign over the weekend because of dwindling munitions.Iran said it had responded by firing on US bases in Jordan and attacking three tankers travelling through the Strait of Hormuz, claiming the vessels had used an unauthorised route.Separately, sources said Saudi Arabia was working to assemble a coalition to protect shipping in the Red Sea from Houthi attacks.The Iran-backed Houthi movement in Yemen had announced on July 20 that it would impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea. The group said it would widen attacks on tankers and also target shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, opening another front in the ongoing Iran war.Meanwhile, though crude prices have once again jumped to the $90 per barrel mark, the spike is still less than the $126 per barrel reached earlier during the conflict.
Article Summary: WTI crude slipped 0.54% to $84.00 a barrel, while Brent crude fell 0.85% to £89.97 a barrel. The decline followed a sharp rebound on Wednesday, when Brent jumped 7.91% and WTI gained 6.56%. The gains had erased the losses from Tuesday, when both benchmarks had dropped about 5%.

Article Title: US Federal Reserve meet today: Kevin Warsh-led FOMC keeps interest rates unchanged
Article Text:
Inflation has remained above the US Fed's 2% target for more than five years. (AP photo)

Kevin Warsh-led Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) decided to keep the interest rate unchanged in the 3.5-3.75% range. The US Federal Reserve announced the monetary policy review after deliberations on July 28 and July 29."The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system," the statement read.“Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty that owes, in part, to the conflict in the Middle East. Productivity growth and capital investment are strong. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little. Inflation remains elevated relative to the Committee’s 2 percent goal, in part reflecting supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy,” the statement added.The US Federal Reserve, which began its two-day policy meeting on Tuesday, was widely expected to leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged.Inflation has remained above the US Fed's 2% target for more than five years. Earlier this month, new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh told Congress that he had “no tolerance’’ for persistently high inflation. This week's meeting is the second monetary policy meeting under his leadership.Oil prices have been highly volatile in recent weeks. Brent crude fell to as low as $72 per barrel earlier this month before surging to $102 last week amid uncertainty over whether the United States and Iran could reach an agreement to restore the free movement of oil tankers through the Middle East.These sharp fluctuations have revived concerns that inflation could accelerate again, just as price pressures had begun easing faster than economists had anticipated.Although higher interest rates help contain inflation, they can also slow economic growth and weigh on stock prices as well as other financial assets.Expensive growth stocks are particularly sensitive to higher borrowing costs, and investors have become increasingly cautious about semiconductor companies and other firms that have benefited from the artificial intelligence boom.Inflation has remained above the Federal Reserve's 2% objective since early 2021, when the US economy rebounded strongly following COVID-19 lockdowns. It peaked at just over 9% in mid-2022 before gradually easing after the Fed raised interest rates 11 times during 2022 and 2023. Since then, however, progress in bringing inflation down has largely stalled.Apart from the conflict involving Iran, inflationary pressures have also been driven by President Donald Trump's tariffs on imported goods and a surge in investment in AI-focused data centres, which has increased demand for computer chips, equipment and electricity.Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, moderated in June, partly because rental inflation slowed. A temporary decline in petrol prices during the month also helped keep overall inflation in check.Even so, several Federal Reserve officials have argued that further interest rate increases may be required to bring inflation back to the central bank's 2% target.
Article Summary: The US Federal Reserve decided to keep the interest rate unchanged in the 3.5-3.75% range. Inflation has remained above the US Fed's 2% target for more than five years. Earlier this month, new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh told Congress that he had “no tolerance’’ for persistently high inflation.

Article Title: Before the knowledge walks out the door
Article Text:
Everyone in Silicon Valley is racing to build machines that replace human expertise.

Ahmer Inam

, a schoolteacher's son from Delhi, is building machines that inherit it.

When Ahmer Inam appeared on Fox & Friends in June, his mother watched the segment without following much of it. Her English is limited. There was her son on the famous curved couch of American morning television, fielding questions about artificial intelligence, and she understood almost none of the words. She wept anyway. Some distances need no translation, and the one between a schoolteacher's household in Delhi and a Manhattan television studio is legible in any language.Had she followed the argument, it might have surprised her less than it surprised the audience. Because what Inam was defending, underneath the vocabulary of frontier AI, is approximately the oldest idea in civilisation — the one his father practised for a living: that knowledge survives only when one generation troubles to hand it to the next.Inam has spent twenty-five years building artificial intelligence — long enough to remember when it meant symbolic logic in the late nineties, and senior enough to have run AI and data for Fortune 500 companies, Nike and Wells Fargo among them, back when "chief AI officer" was still an exotic title. He is not, in other words, a critic sniping from the cheap seats. Which makes the thesis of Cognisee, the research lab he founded and leads, sound almost seditious in today's Silicon Valley: "We're not trying to replace the worker," he says."We're trying to make the worker irreplaceable."The problem he is aiming at usually gets filed under the bland heading of "labour shortage." By one estimate, more than two million skilled-trade jobs in the United States could sit unfilled by 2030 — electricians, welders, machinists, the hands America needs if it is serious about building factories, chip plants and grid capacity again. But Inam's diagnosis is sharper than a headcount. "America does not have a work shortage," he likes to say. "It has an expertise shortage."Consider what actually leaves the building when a master electrician retires at sixty-eight. Not the manual — the manual stays. What leaves is the ear that catches a motor running slightly wrong two weeks before it fails; the instinct that connects a faint vibration to a pattern in old maintenance logs; forty years of judgment that was never written down because it could not be. The philosopher Michael Polanyi had a name for this — tacit knowledge, the things we know but cannot tell — and Cognisee is, at bottom, a bet that the most valuable training data on earth is tacit.The company's method has a fable-like symmetry. Its AI begins as an apprentice: it works alongside experienced people and learns what they notice, what they ask, how they make judgment calls. Then it turns around and becomes a coach, carrying that accumulated judgment to the newcomer. "First it's an apprentice," Inam says. "Then it becomes a coach." Picture a 22-year-old on his first aircraft-maintenance job, hearing a sound he has never heard before, with the distilled instincts of the country's best technicians beside him in real time. "He's not being replaced by a machine," Inam says. "He's being mentored by one."The repository where all this lives is called, a little grandly, a Wisdom Vault — a secure library of hard-won know-how from doctors, nurses, electricians, factory workers, farmers, small-business owners. Grand or not, the name gives away the emotional register Inam is working in. This is not pitched as workforce optimisation. It is pitched as inheritance.He is careful — insistent, actually — about the question that framing invites: who owns it? In Cognisee's design, the expert decides what to preserve, what to share, and with whom; the contributor is recognised and rewarded; the knowledge belongs to the person who earned it, not to the machine that absorbed it. "There is a big difference," Inam says, "between being monitored and being mentored." The company is incorporated as a public benefit corporation, which he describes as a legal commitment to the worker rather than a marketing pledge.That ownership principle is also where his quarrel with the reigning AI paradigm becomes explicit. The frontier labs, Inam argues, got intelligent by swallowing the written internet — and the written internet is now substantially swallowed, which is why the industry's plan increasingly amounts to bigger data centres and more electricity, even as some of the field's own pioneers warn of a wall ahead. His contrarian wager is that the next leap will come not from more compute but from the knowledge that never made it onto the internet in the first place — and that it can be gathered by consent rather than by crawler.For an Indian reader, the resonance is hard to miss. This is a country that has watched its weaves, its remedies and its craft knowledge catalogued, carried off and sold back to it before. It is also a country whose deepest teaching traditions were never textual at all, but moved from person to person — the guru-shishya parampara, the ustad and the shagird. Inam has spoken about Wisdom Vaults for indigenous and medicinal knowledge, with communities retaining ownership of what they contribute. One way to describe Cognisee is as an attempt to give the world's oral inheritances an infrastructure layer — sovereignty included.The idea is attracting converts from unexpected quarters. Cognisee's co-founder, Alex Giannou, spent nearly two decades on Wall Street financing precisely the data centres and power deals behind the AI boom; he crossed over, in Inam's telling, because the right bet and the smart bet turned out to be the same one. Among the company's early backers is a senior Google executive who helped invent federated learning, one of the foundational privacy-preserving techniques of modern machine learning. And last year the XPRIZE Foundation, where Inam serves as a Visionary, recognised his work with its Global Visioneering Award.None of which quite explains the conviction. For that you have to go back to Delhi. Inam grew up in a low-income household, the son of a teacher — a man who spent his working life on the least scalable expertise-transfer technology ever devised: one adult, one room, one generation at a time. The son's journey to America was not gilded; there were stretches, early on, when he could not always afford to eat. It takes a particular kind of person to emerge from that and conclude that a nation's most undervalued asset sits not in its server farms but in the heads of its retiring machinists and nurses."Every generation should start where the last one left off," Inam says. It sounds like a product principle. It is closer to a family creed — the thing his father practised without ever calling it a thesis, the thing his mother recognised on a television screen in a language she does not speak. Some knowledge, it turns out, transfers just fine.
Article Summary: Ahmer Inam, a schoolteacher's son from Delhi, is building machines that inherit it. The problem he is aiming at usually gets filed under the bland heading of "labour shortage" By one estimate, more than two million skilled-trade jobs in the United States could sit unfilled by 2030.

Article Title: EU's new salary transparency rules: 'Pay has long been treated as deeply personal'
Article Text:
The law behind the numbers

Not just a gender story

The hardest part isn't the spreadsheet

Your compensation model defines the workforce you attract

Why the law alone won't close the gap

Losse's real fix: Three things, not one

Across the European Union, women earn on average 11.1% less per hour than men. In India, government figures show male salaried workers earning roughly 24% more than their female counterparts. In the United States, women took home about 85 cents for every dollar men earned in 2024, per the Pew Research Center.The comparative numbers explain why a new EU law is being watched well beyond Europe. For decades, the gap has persisted partly because pay was rarely open to scrutiny; what colleagues earned, and why, stayed behind closed doors. That is about to change in Europe, where a sweeping new regulation is forcing companies to open their books on who earns what, and why.At its core, the directive is designed to make it harder for pay inequity to hide in plain sight. Its stated goal is to strengthen the principle of equal pay for equal work, or work of equal value, by giving employees the information and legal standing to check whether their own pay is fair.Formally Directive requires companies across the European Union's 27 member states to disclose pay ranges to job applicants, ban questions about salary history, and give employees the right to ask what colleagues doing equal work earn.Larger employers must also publish gender pay gap data every one to three years, and build a “job evaluation” system, using objective, gender-neutral criteria such as skill, responsibility, effort and working conditions, that explains why one role pays more than another. Where the unexplained gap within a job category exceeds 5%, employers must address it, with worker representatives, within six months.Member states were required to transpose the directive into national law by June 7, 2026. By that deadline, according to law firm trackers, only a handful of countries, among them Italy and Slovakia, had full implementing legislation in force. Economies including Germany, France, Spain, Austria and the Netherlands had missed it outright, with Brussels signalling that infringement proceedings could follow.When Tanja Losse and her team at Eurogroup Consulting ran a full job evaluation across a European financial services firm's workforce earlier this year, benchmarking every role against the market and against internal peers doing comparable work, the results surprised her. A significant share of employees, considerably more than her client had anticipated, turned out to be paid less than their role and level warranted, not because anyone had deliberately shortchanged them, but because, in many cases, nobody had ever formally checked.“Pay has historically been treated as something deeply personal, almost taboo to discuss,” explains Losse, a strategy consultant for financial services at Eurogroup Consulting who has spent much of the past year helping European banks prepare for a new EU regulation whose implications reach well beyond compliance and into business strategy. “In practice, what someone ends up earning has often come down to how well they negotiated, rather than the role itself or how they perform in it. ”Losse's case findings complicate the assumption that pay inequity is simply a story about women being underpaid relative to men. Among the employees she identified as underpaid, the split between men and women was close to even, roughly half and half. What differed was the size of the gap: among underpaid women, the shortfall relative to what their role warranted was consistently larger than among underpaid men, even though similar numbers of each were affected. “It tells you this isn't purely a gender issue, it's a negotiation and structural issue that happens to hit women harder,” Losse notes.Losse says the technical side of a project like this, pulling the data, running the job evaluation, is the easier half. What decides whether it actually works is who backs it and how carefully the result gets delivered. In her experience, that means keeping the chief executive close with regular updates, and treating the works council and the company's controlling function as partners rather than checkboxes to clear.The group most often overlooked, she says, is the one with the most at stake: the employees themselves, some of whom fear the audit will mean they end up earning less. That is why she treats the communication around a project like this as being just as important as the analysis itself.One discovery from her most recent project reshaped how her team ran it. The leadership team turned out to be far less consistent than expected: some managers held regular, structured conversations with their staff about performance, others held almost none. That gap mattered because those same managers would have to deliver the audit's most sensitive finding directly to each employee, which pay bracket they now sat in, and what their development path looked like from there.Losse's team responded by building a dedicated coaching programme to prepare managers for those conversations, including the pushback some were likely to face. She now treats how well a leadership team handles that individual conversation as one of the clearest predictors of whether a pay equity project succeeds or quietly fails. The measurable result, she says, was a completely rebuilt compensation framework, covering salary and every other monetary benefit, delivered within a year, an ambitious timeline for an organisation of that size and complexity.On paper, implementing a regulation like this can look like a purely technical exercise: pull the pay data, run the numbers, file the report. Losse pushes back on that framing. In her experience, it is at its core a change and communication programme, one that ends up shaping the workforce a company will have five or ten years from now, including who it keeps, who it promotes and who it can attract in the first place.“People treat this as a data or IT migration project. It isn't. It's setting the path for the workforce you want to keep, promote and attract,” Losse insists.That strategic weight shows up most clearly in how a compensation model actually gets designed, she says. Fairness demands rules that apply uniformly, the same bonus structure for everyone in a given role, for instance, so pay cannot simply come down to who negotiates hardest. But a model built only on uniform rules risks flattening the one thing that keeps ambitious employees engaged: a visible path for growth.The harder design problem, in her view, is building in enough structure to guarantee fairness while leaving room for a development track that rewards learning and growth, and enough flexibility to retain or reward the highest performers. “If you make it completely rigid, you lose the ability to develop and motivate people, and you risk losing your high potentials. If you make it too flexible, you're back to the same inconsistency the law is trying to fix. Getting that balance right is the hardest part of the whole design,” she adds.That, she contends, is why the exercise is worth doing even for companies outside the EU with no legal obligation to run one. The underlying questions, how to define fair pay, how to keep a visible development path open, and how to stay flexible enough to compete for talent, are workforce strategy questions every company eventually has to answer, regulation or not.That question already has an answer, of sorts, in parts of the world with no EU-style mandate. In the United States, roughly 19 states, including California, Colorado, New York and Illinois, require salary ranges in job postings, but there is no federal law and no single national standard. India's Code on Wages, 2019, already requires equal pay for equal work, but it carries no requirement to disclose pay data or ranges, leaving enforcement to inspection and individual complaint rather than routine transparency.Even full compliance, Losse argues, will not by itself close Europe's pay gap. The directive addresses pay gaps within a given role or job level; it does little about the fact that women remain underrepresented in the highest-paid roles in the first place, a pattern researchers call occupational segregation.The 2025 Women in the Workplace report found that for every 100 men promoted to manager, only 89 white women and 54 Black women received the same promotion, a bottleneck at the first rung of management, not the top, that compounds over a career.Losse points to two structural levers she considers more consequential than transparency law alone: childcare and reskilling. Affordable, accessible childcare, she argues, determines whether women can stay on a career track at all, rather than trading progression for flexibility.And as generative AI reshapes which roles survive, employers need to actively invest in moving workers out of the roles most exposed to automation and into higher-value, higher-paid ones. Research led by Stanford economist Erik Brynjolfsson found that employment for early-career workers, ages 22 to 25, in the most AI-exposed occupations has fallen roughly 13% since 2022, even as employment for older workers in the same fields grew, a divergence that has held for nearly four years with no sign of reversing.“If we don't actively help people in at-risk roles move up the skills ladder, transparency on today's pay structure won't matter much, because the structure itself is about to shift,” Losse says.Losse's bottom line is less about any single law than about sequencing. Pay transparency, she says, is a genuinely useful first step: it forces companies to justify pay decisions they may never have examined, and it takes the negotiation advantage away from whoever is simply better at asking. But on its own, it will not close a gap rooted as much in who gets promoted and who can afford to stay in the workforce as in what any individual is paid for a given role.“Transparency, childcare access and a genuine commitment to reskilling, those three things together are what actually move the number,” she concludes.For Losse, the interest is not purely professional. Financial literacy has mattered to her since early in her career, when she volunteered teaching children about money, and giving people a fair, transparent stake in their own finances is a large part of what drives her.It is also why she pays close attention to research like Brynjolfsson's: the question she thinks companies and employees now have to answer together is which skills, among them leadership, empathy, communication and the ability to keep learning, will keep a workforce relevant as AI reshapes which jobs remain.(Tanja Losse is a strategy consultant for financial services at Eurogroup Consulting, where she advises banks on strategy, transformation and organisational change.)
Article Summary: Women earn on average 11.1% less per hour than men in the European Union. In India, government figures show male salaried workers earning roughly 24% more than their female counterparts. In the United States, women took home about 85 cents for every dollar men earned in 2024.

Article Title: Oil prices jump over 7% as Middle East chaos flares up, brent crude back at $90 per barrel
Article Text: Oil prices rallied sharply on Wednesday, with benchmark crude contracts gaining over 7%, after a fresh wave of military action in the Middle East reignited concerns over global oil supplies. The rally was also supported by industry data showing a drawdown in US crude inventories.Around 9 pm IST, Brent crude rose $6.28, or 7.47%, to $90.37 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) gained $5.67, or 7.15%, to $84.93 a barrel.The latest jump followed renewed strikes involving the United States, Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed groups, reversing expectations that the US-Israeli war with Iran could soon move towards a resolution."Renewed military strikes in the Middle East and Iranian officials reiterating that they want to control shipping activity through the Strait of Hormuz amid depressed oil flows through the Strait are lifting oil prices again," UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo told Reuters.The United States and Saudi Arabia carried out strikes on Iran-backed groups in Iraq on Wednesday, saying the groups were responsible for drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities.Earlier, the US military said that it had prevented what it described as a surprise Iranian attack on American troops in the region. Iran, in turn, said it had targeted ships in the Strait of Hormuz and US bases in Jordan.Markets found further support after US President Donald Trump said in an interview with Fox News that the United States would respond with retaliatory strikes against Iran.The developments also dealt a blow to diplomatic efforts around the Strait of Hormuz. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran had rejected Oman's proposal for regional joint management of the strategic waterway, dimming hopes of resolving a months-long impasse that has disrupted Gulf trade.The disruption has continued to affect shipping. Only a small number of commodity vessels have crossed the Strait of Hormuz this week. By comparison, traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait increased, with five ships passing through on Wednesday and 39 on Tuesday, the highest daily count since July 19, before Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia.According to regional sources cited by Reuters, the Houthis are also considering imposing charges on commercial vessels using the southern Red Sea. Six sources familiar with the matter also said China has held direct discussions with the group to ensure its oil tankers can transit the route without being attacked.Analysts said oil prices are likely to remain volatile as the conflict continues to shift."We believe Brent oil prices will continue to whipsaw in the $80-$100 per barrel range in the near term as the conflict ebbs and flows in the Middle East," said Suvro Sarkar, head of energy research at DBS Bank."The situation has escalated since US President Donald Trump signalled a return to diplomacy earlier in the week," he said."This series of stop-start negotiations means a complete removal of the Strait of Hormuz blockade is not achieved, and oil prices could see higher floor of around $80 per barrel even under a de-escalation scenario."Apart from geopolitical tensions, traders also drew support from inventory data. Market sources, citing figures from the American Petroleum Institute, said US crude stockpiles declined by about 3.3 million barrels during the week ended July 24. Official figures from the Energy Information Administration are expected later on Wednesday.
Article Summary: Brent crude rose $6.28, or 7.47%, to $90.37 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) gained 7.15, to $84.93 a barrel. The latest jump followed renewed strikes involving the United States, Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed groups.

Article Title: US stock market today: Wall Street in red ahead of US Federal Reserve policy review; oil prices climb
Article Text:
Technology stocks, particularly companies viewed as richly valued, remain under pressure.

US stock market today: US equities traded in negative on Wednesday as investors awaited the outcome of the Federal Reserve's latest policy meeting on interest rates. Meanwhile, oil prices climbed sharply.S&P 500 edged down 0.73%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost over 700 points, or 1.42%, while the Nasdaq Composite managed a also dropped 1.05%The biggest moves were seen in the energy market. Brent crude surged 5.6% to $86.64 a barrel after fresh hostilities involving Iran heightened concerns over global oil supplies. Iran launched a missile attack on US forces in the Middle East, while US forces, alongside Saudi Arabia, carried out strikes on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.Oil prices have been highly volatile in recent weeks. Brent crude had fallen to around $72 a barrel earlier this month before briefly touching $102 last week as uncertainty persisted over whether Washington and Tehran could reach an agreement that would allow oil shipments from the Middle East to resume without disruption.The renewed rise in crude prices has fuelled concerns that inflation could accelerate again after showing signs of easing faster than expected.That uncertainty has also complicated expectations ahead of the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision following the conclusion of its two-day policy meeting, according to an AP report.Markets are currently assigning about a 36% probability to a US rate hike, which, if delivered, would mark the first increase in three years. While higher interest rates help curb inflation, they can also dampen economic activity and weigh on equity valuations.Technology stocks, particularly companies viewed as richly valued, remain under pressure. Investors have become increasingly cautious about semiconductor manufacturers and other beneficiaries of the artificial intelligence boom, amid concerns that the rapid pace of earnings growth may not be sustainable if AI fails to deliver the expected gains in profitability and productivity.The shift in sentiment was especially evident in South Korea, where the stock market is heavily influenced by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The KOSPI index fell another 6% after plunging 10.8% in the previous session, reducing its gains for the year to 34.4%.SK Hynix shares dropped 9.6%. Although the company reported record quarterly revenue and profit driven by strong AI-related demand, its 257% revenue growth still failed to meet analysts' expectations.Elsewhere, global markets presented a mixed picture. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index advanced 2%, while France's CAC 40 declined 0.7%.In the bond market, US Treasury yields moved slightly higher alongside rising oil prices. The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note inched up to 4.62% from 4.61% at Tuesday's close.
Article Summary: S&P 500 edged down 0.73%. Dow Jones Industrial Average lost over 700 points, or 1.42%. Nasdaq Composite managed a also dropped 1.05%. Brent crude surged 5.6% to $86.64 a barrel after fresh hostilities involving Iran.

Article Title: South Korea's Kospi tumbles 6% as SK Hynix slide, AI spending worries trigger chip selloff
Article Text:
A screen shows the Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) at the Korea Exchange in Seoul, South Korea, Wednesday, July 29, 2026. (AP Photo)

South Korea's benchmark Kospi index plunged 6% on Wednesday, dragged down by a sharp selloff in chipmakers after SK Hynix reported quarterly earnings that, despite surging nearly sixfold from a year ago, missed analysts' expectations.The benchmark index had fallen more than 8 per cent during intraday trade before recovering some losses to close at 5,663.24, its lowest level since early April. The decline came just days after the Kospi had climbed above the 9,000 mark.Shares of memory chip giant SK Hynix tumbled 9.4 per cent after its operating profit for the latest quarter fell short of market forecasts. Samsung Electronics also lost 4.8 per cent, adding to pressure on the index.The selloff reflects renewed investor concerns over lofty valuations of artificial intelligence-linked stocks, particularly semiconductor companies that have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom.Markets have been hit by repeated bouts of profit-taking in AI-related shares amid growing doubts over whether massive investments in artificial intelligence will generate the expected returns.Investor sentiment has also been dented by China's progress in developing lower-cost advanced AI models, raising concerns over future demand and profitability for premium chipmakers.The weakness spread across the region, with Japan's Nikkei 225 falling 1.5 per cent as chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron slumped 10.6 per cent and Lasertec Corp. dropped 8.3 per cent. Taiwan's Taiex also declined 3.8 per cent.Broader Asian markets were mixed. Hong Kong's Hang Seng gained 1.8 per cent, while China's Shanghai Composite rose 0.4 per cent. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 advanced 1% after inflation data eased concerns over further interest-rate hikes, and India's Sensex traded 1.1 per cent higher.On Wall Street overnight, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.2 per cent as AI-related stocks remained under pressure. Micron Technology fell 8.9 per cent, while Advanced Micro Devices and Applied Materials dropped 8.1 per cent and 7.8 per cent, respectively, reflecting continued investor caution toward semiconductor stocks despite generally strong corporate earnings.
Article Summary: The benchmark index had fallen more than 8 per cent during intraday trade before recovering some losses to close at 5,663.24. The decline came just days after the Kospi had climbed above the 9,000 mark. Shares of memory chip giant SK Hynix tumbled 9.4 per cent after its operating profit fell short of market forecasts.

Article Title: Crude prices climb over 4% as renewed Middle East tensions, inventory draw fuel supply fears
Article Text: Oil prices rebounded sharply on Wednesday, reversing part of the previous session's steep decline, as renewed tensions in the Middle East reignited concerns over global crude supplies. Lower US crude inventories and expectations around OPEC+ production policy also lent support to the market.Brent crude climbed 4.41% to $87.80 a barrel, gaining $3.71, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose 4.23%, or $3.35, to $82.61 a barrel.The market had retreated nearly 5% on Tuesday, touching a two-week low after hopes emerged that the pause in hostilities between Washington and Tehran could pave the way for renewed diplomatic engagement. Those expectations were tempered as the regional security situation deteriorated once again.Fresh concerns centred on the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil shipping route. Any prolonged disruption in the waterway could raise energy costs further, increase transportation expenses, push fuel prices higher and add inflationary pressure across major economies.Military developments in the region also remained in focus.Saudi Arabia said that it had joined the US Central Command (CENTCOM) in carrying out air strikes on Iran-backed militant targets in Iraq after recent drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities. The Saudi defence ministry said that the kingdom was not seeking escalation but would respond to actions threatening its security and critical infrastructure.CENTCOM said the joint operation targeted multiple Iran-aligned militant logistics and weapons sites in eastern Iraq on July 28 after more than 30 IRGC-directed drone attacks were launched over the previous 72 hours against US forces and Saudi energy infrastructure.At the same time, signs of tighter US crude supplies added to bullish sentiment. Market sources, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute, said US crude inventories fell by around 3.3 million barrels in the week ended July 24. Gasoline stocks, however, increased by 918,000 barrels, while distillate inventories rose by 355,000 barrels from the previous week. Official data from the Energy Information Administration is due later on Wednesday.The rising tensions have also prompted shipping companies operating in the Gulf to remain on alert. Several operators have altered sailing routes, tightened onboard security measures and reassessed insurance coverage amid fears of further attacks on commercial vessels.Oil prices also found support from expectations that OPEC+ could pause planned production increases for three months from October after completing the scheduled return of barrels following voluntary output cuts.The market has remained highly volatile amid the US-Israeli war in Iran, which has disrupted global crude flows, particularly following the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.US President Donald Trump, who called off a two-week US bombing campaign over the weekend, told Fox News on Tuesday that there were "good talks" with Iran, while warning that more strikes could follow if negotiations fail. Iran, however, denied that it is seeking to resume talks with the United States.
Article Summary: Brent crude climbed 4.41% to $87.80 a barrel, gaining $3.71. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose 4.23%, or £3.35, to $82.61 a barrel. The market had retreated nearly 5% on Tuesday, touching a two-week low.

Article Title: US stock market today: S&P 500, Dow Jones trade flat; Nasdaq drops over 1% as chips stocks drop
Article Text:
Lofty expectations have placed particular pressure on semiconductor companies and other firms that have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the artificial intelligence boom.

US stock market today: Most Wall Street indices traded higher on Tuesday, although semiconductor stocks continued to face heavy selling across global markets. Oil prices also extended their decline after retreating from the two-month highs reached last week.In early trading, the S&P 500 was little changed, masking significant divergence across sectors. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 385 points, or 0.7%, while the Nasdaq Composite slipped over 1%, according to an AP report.Broader market sentiment remained supported by another round of stronger-than-expected corporate earnings. Coca-Cola advanced 5.8% after reporting a 7% increase in revenue, despite what Chief Executive Officer Henrique Braun described as “a dynamic consumer landscape.”Sherwin-Williams climbed 7% and Illinois Tool Works added 3.7% after both companies posted quarterly profits that exceeded analysts' expectations. Over the longer term, stock prices tend to track corporate earnings, and expectations have remained elevated as US equities continue to trade close to record highs.Those lofty expectations have placed particular pressure on semiconductor companies and other firms that have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the artificial intelligence boom.Micron Technology, for instance, has seen its share price more than triple this year following exceptionally strong growth. During the quarter ended May 28, the company reported revenue that was more than four times higher than a year earlier.However, investors are increasingly questioning whether such rapid expansion can be sustained. Concerns have emerged that major spending on memory chips could slow if artificial intelligence fails to deliver the expected gains in profitability or productivity. At the same time, lower-cost AI models emerging from China could reduce demand for memory chips and conventional computing power.Micron's shares fell 8.4%, making it the biggest drag on the S&P 500. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) declined 7.7%, while Nvidia lost 1.1%, adding to the weakness in the technology sector.The selloff was even more pronounced in overseas markets earlier in the day. Sharp declines in SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics pulled South Korea's KOSPI index down 10.8%, with losses severe enough to trigger temporary trading halts in Seoul.“We believe the market was likely spooked by the progress of China’s chipmaking equipment capabilities, and was worried that this progress would threaten the competitive position of global chipmaking and chip equipment leaders,” said equity analyst Jing Jie Yu of Morningstar.“That said, we believe the sell-off today is largely a knee-jerk reaction and overdone,” he said, adding that the leadership position of the world's major chipmakers is unlikely to face any meaningful threat.In the commodities market, Brent crude for October delivery fell 2.2% to $83.97 a barrel. Just last week, the September contract had briefly surged to as high as $102 per barrel amid concerns that the conflict in the Middle East could disrupt global crude supplies.The decline in oil prices also supported the bond market. The yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note eased to 4.62% from 4.65% at Monday's close.
Article Summary: Most Wall Street indices traded higher on Tuesday, although semiconductor stocks continued to face heavy selling across global markets. Oil prices also extended their decline after retreating from the two-month highs reached last week. Broader market sentiment remained supported by another round of stronger-than- expected corporate earnings.

Article Title: 1.14 lakh startups generate more than 12 lakh jobs in India: Finance ministry
Article Text:
Finance Ministry

NEW DELHI: More than 1.14 lakh startups in India have created over 12 lakh jobs so far, the finance ministry said in its latest review of the Indian economy.In the report titled, ‘The Indian Economy: A Review January 2024’, the Department of Economic Affairs said that the 1.14 lakh startups recognised by the government under the 'Startup India initiative’ created more than 12 lakh jobs (as of October 2023).The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023, the document read.Despite facing global challenges in 2023 like valuation issues, few IPOs, regulatory changes and macroeconomic and geopolitical trends, India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year.The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion (from 2019 to 2023), according to a recent report by Nasscom in collaboration with Zinnov.“In 2023, despite facing global economic and regulatory challenges, Indian tech startups have prioritised the imperative of enhancing their business fundamentals, driving profitability and growth,” said Debjani Ghosh, President, Nasscom.“The proliferation of tech startups in tier 2 and 3 cities marks the ecosystem's resilience,” she added.Navigating 2024, tech startup founders expect to continue the revenue growth path with measured steps focusing on optimising expenditure and maximising profitability for B2B tech startups.Investments in deeptech will continue an upward trend in 2024. With generative AI (GenAI) acceleration, 70 per cent of start-up founders are embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in their solutions.As funding becomes scarce for the Indian startup ecosystem in general, the explosion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has given a new lease of life to entrepreneurs and founders in the country, as the Centre extends support to the sector.
Article Summary: The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023. India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year. The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion.
